briefRows.brief: Beat 4 caption: Nelson's fleet 'linked to the coast by a chain of frigates'
briefRows.sources: Frigates (Euryalus, Sirius, Phoebe, Naiad) held only the Cádiz end. The outer links were ships of the line: the Defence, Colossus and Mars, with the Agamemnon stationed beside the Defence (Nelson's diary, 14 October, Hudson 1917, p. 21; Beatty 1807, p. 6; memorandum of 20 October, Nicolas VII 136). The Mars passed the signal to the Victory (Hudson 1917, p. 22; Cumby 1899, p. 719)
briefRows.scene: Caption: 'a chain of frigates and ships of the line' (or 'a chain of ships'). Frigate glyphs inshore, ship-of-the-line glyphs further out

briefRows.brief: Concept and beat 4: the chain 'lights up ship by ship when the combined fleet sails'
briefRows.sources: The relay of 19 October ran in daylight, 7 to 9.30 a.m. It used numeral flags and Popham's telegraph, kept flying until repeated, with counted guns and the Phoebe's three-minute guns. The last link, the Mars, was hull-down from the fleet and switched to a colour-blind distant signal of a flag, a ball and a pendant (Cumby 1899, p. 719). Blue lights, rockets and gun flashes belong to the nights of 19–20 and 20–21 October
briefRows.scene: By day each link 'lights up' as a flag hoist and white gun puffs, held until the Victory answers; light effects only in the night beat

briefRows.brief: Beat 4: 'The fleet comes out and the chain lights up'; caption: 'the signal runs down the chain'
briefRows.sources: The signal went out as the first ships got under way (the northernmost at 7 a.m.); only seven of the line got out that day, the rest on the 20th (research/scene-02/a-h2c.md, H2-30c). On the logged clocks it took about 2½ hours (range 2 h to about 3¼ h) to cover 48–58 nm (research/scene-02/a-h3.md, R2, R10)
briefRows.scene: Discrete pulses with pauses, never instant: 7 a.m. at Cádiz, 9.30 at the Victory. Captions say 'by half past nine', never 'in minutes' or 'within two hours'
briefRows.confidence: High for the sequence, medium for the duration

briefRows.brief: Concept: 'the chain of ships between the harbour and Nelson's fleet'; history: the frigates signal the enemy's movements through the night of 20 to 21 October
briefRows.sources: There were two different chains. On 19 October a line of 48–58 nm ran about due west (true) of Cádiz. On the night of 20–21 October Nelson's memorandum set a short chain between the converging fleets, south-west of Cádiz and away from the harbour: the Euryalus and Sirius by the enemy, then the Phoebe and Naiad, then the Defence, Colossus and Mars to the Victory. It was under 10 nm in all, and some links worked by hailing (Nicolas VII 136; NRS II 149, 245, 303, 306)
briefRows.scene: Beat 4: the long day chain west of Cádiz. Beat 5: a short night chain between the fleets, led by hourly paired blue lights
briefRows.confidence: High for the stations, low for the night distances

fleetRows.stage: Off Cádiz, morning of 19 October (the relay)
fleetRows.shipsOfTheLine: 27 in all (Nicolas VII 130; Browne, NRS II 194; Cumby 1899, p. 718), as in research/scene-02/a-h2b.md, H2-19a. This part adds the split. Beatty (1807, p. 6) puts four in the cordon (Colossus, Mars, Defence, Agamemnon), which leaves 23 lying to with Nelson. The Agamemnon's part in the relay is unproven (a-h3.md, R6), so 23–24 were with Nelson and 3–4 in the chain. Walker's 26 'under all sail' (NRS II 323) is the low count
fleetRows.others: Inshore: the frigates Euryalus, Sirius, Phoebe and Naiad; the brig Weazle and the schooner Pickle, both sent away that morning (NRS II 146). With the fleet: the cutter Entreprenante
fleetRows.sources: Nicolas VII 130; NRS II 146, 194, 323; Beatty 1807, p. 6; Cumby 1899, p. 718; research/scene-02/a-h3.md, R6–R7
fleetRows.confidence: High for 27; medium for the split between the fleet and the chain

fleetRows.shipsOfTheLine: 27: the Defence, Colossus and Mars as links (memorandum of 20 October, Nicolas VII 136) and 24 with Nelson. The Africa missed the 8 p.m. wear and held on north out of touch (Corbett 1910, p. 340)
fleetRows.others: Frigates Euryalus and Sirius by the enemy, Phoebe and Naiad between; the schooner Pickle with the Sirius (NRS II 317); the cutter Entreprenante
fleetRows.confidence: High for the stations; medium for which ships were where

dates.event: The Sirius telegraphs that the enemy have hoisted their topsail yards: the first signal of the sortie
dates.alternatives: 6.04 a.m. in the Euryalus's signal log (NRS II 160); 'six o'clock' in Corbett 1910, p. 333; entered under the 'At 4' (morning watch) heading in the Sirius's log (NRS II 312)

dates.event: No. 370, 'the enemy's ships are coming out of port', from the Sirius to the Euryalus, then to the Phoebe at 7.20: the relay begins (the hour is optional on the date line)
dates.alternatives: 7.00 by the Euryalus's clock (NRS II 160). Corbett's 'in ten minutes' (7.10) for the Phoebe has no support in the logs, which give 7.20

dates.event: The Mars's signal reaches the Victory, which answers and makes the general chase in the SE quarter (the hour is optional on the date line)
dates.alternatives: 9.30 by the Victory's clock (Hudson 1917, p. 22; Beatty 1807, p. 7; James III 389); 10 a.m. (Lt Browne, NRS II 194); 'about nine' (Walker, NRS II 322); about 10.15 local time if the Victory's clock ran 45 minutes slow (research/scene-02/a-h3.md, R10)

dates.event: Nelson's memorandum sets the night chain and the code of two blue lights, or three guns, every hour
Nelson signals that he relies on Blackwood to keep sight of the enemy; the Naiad reports 31 sail NNE
dates.alternatives: 6 p.m. for the Naiad in Nicolas VII 137, from a facsimile; 5.40 by the Euryalus's clock for Nelson's signal (NRS II 149); 'a little before sunset' (Beatty 1807, p. 9)

dates.event: The night chain at work: paired blue lights, rockets and guns from about 6 p.m. and through the night of 20–21 October
dates.alternatives: The date line turns to 21 October 1805 at dawn

dates.event: The British fleet wears to the SW by Night Signal No. 31; the Victory burns blue lights to show her position
dates.alternatives: 8.40 p.m. (James III 390)

dates.event: The British fleet wears to the NE
dates.alternatives: About 2 a.m. in Beatty's narrative (1807, p. 11), against his own appendix and the logs; 4.20 (Dreadnought, Conqueror) and 4.30 (Phoebe) by their own clocks

positions.what: Sirius, inshore frigate: telegraph at 6.04, No. 370 at 7.00
positions.note: Cádiz NE by E, 4 miles (NRS II 312), corrected for 20–21° W. About 33 m deep today (EMODnet)

positions.what: Euryalus (Blackwood), receives No. 370 and passes it to the Phoebe
positions.note: San Sebastián NE, about 4 miles (NRS II 145). About 32 m deep today

positions.what: Euryalus at noon, with the Sirius in company
positions.note: San Sebastián E ½ N, 7 or 8 miles; latitude observed 36°28′ N (NRS II 146)

positions.what: Naiad, repeating between the Euryalus and the Phoebe from 8.10
positions.note: San Sebastián light 11 or 12 miles (NRS II 302); NW by W by compass of the Sirius (NRS II 312); research/scene-02/a-h2b.md, H2-37e

positions.what: Phoebe, sent west at 7.20 'firing three minute guns'
positions.note: WNW by compass (due west true) of the Euryalus at 8; beyond the Naiad at noon. a-h2b.md, H2-37e gives 36.50–36.55 N, 6.6–6.75 W. A moving link: nearer the Euryalus earlier in the morning

positions.what: Defence, innermost ship of the line (the Agamemnon, optional, beside her)
positions.note: 'west' by compass from the Euryalus's masthead puts her at 36.32–36.42 N (a-h2b.md, H2-37f). Her usual station on the parallel would be 36.53 N 6.85 W (a-h2c.md, H2-40c), but there she would have borne WNW. About 457 m deep today

positions.what: Colossus, inferred link
positions.note: Between the Defence and the Mars (inferred); the 14 October diary has her with the Mars, 5 leagues east of the fleet

positions.what: Mars, last link: hull-down from the fleet, makes the distant signal
positions.note: 5 leagues east of the fleet (diary, 14 Oct); a-h2c.md, H2-40c puts the Mars and Colossus at 7.06–7.09 W; hull-down from the Bellerophon (Cumby 1899, p. 719)

positions.what: Victory and the main body, lying to; general chase at 9.30
positions.spread: 23–24 ships of the line in loose cruising order around the Victory, a few nm across
positions.note: Between Nelson's 16 leagues ESE by compass (36°34′ N 7°18′ W) and the noon log position (36°36′ N 7°30′ W; Corbett 1910, p. 333 n. 1). After 9.30 the fleet headed E by S, then SE by E by compass (Téméraire's log), about 80–105° true. About 477 m deep today

positions.what: Phoebe, linking frigate, burning blue lights and rockets
positions.note: Cádiz lighthouse E by N, about 5 leagues (NRS II 306)

positions.what: Combined Fleet, centre of its line (reference for the night chain)
positions.spread: 33 of the line, 5 frigates and 2 brigs in a ragged line about 6 nm long, roughly N–S, on the starboard tack, showing stern and top lights
positions.note: Interpolated (research/scene-02/h2-boulogne-cadiz.md, section 9.4). Night course SW by S by compass, about S by W true (a-h2c.md, H2-31g). Draw loosely and anchor on the dawn positions (a-h2c.md, H2-32i)

positions.what: Euryalus, on the enemy's weather beam
positions.note: The enemy's body SE by S (NRS II 149) or SE by E (Nicolas VII 134 n.), about 3 miles

positions.what: Sirius, by the enemy, burning blue lights and rockets and firing guns
positions.note: The enemy east, 4 miles (NRS II 313); east, six miles, at 11.30 in the extract in Nicolas VII 134 n.

positions.what: The light of the British fleet (presumably the Victory's)
positions.note: To the southward and westward of the Euryalus, 5 or 6 miles (NRS II 149). After the 8 p.m. wear the fleet stood SW by compass, about SSW true. At 4 a.m. the Mars had the Victory WSW, 3 or 4 miles (NRS II 245)

openDoubts: Which ships of the line passed No. 370 on 19 October. The Defence and Colossus are inferred. The Agamemnon was stationed in the cordon (Beatty 1807, p. 6; James III 389), but nothing shows she relayed the signal (research/scene-02/a-h3.md, R5–R6).

How long the relay took. The logged clocks give about 2½ hours. Blackwood's 'within two hours' is the short end; Corbett's 45-minute clock offset, found on the 20th, gives about 3¼ hours. For the arrival, Browne gives 10 a.m. and Walker 'about nine' (a-h3.md, R10).

Where the Victory lay at 9.30. Nelson's 16 leagues ESE by compass gives about 36°34′ N 7°18′ W. The noon log position is 36°36′ N 7°30′ W, 19 leagues off, although the fleet had chased east in light airs since 9.30.

Where the Defence lay at 8 a.m. The Euryalus's masthead bearing ('west' by compass) puts her about 10 nm south of Cádiz's parallel (a-h2b.md, H2-37f). Nelson's 'in the latitude' order and her usual station put her on it (a-h2c.md, H2-40c).
The Mars's distant signal (a flag, a ball and a pendant) rests on one eyewitness writing years later (Cumby). No printed description of the 1805 Distant Signals was found.

Night of 20–21 October: whether the frigates also used the 1799 book's tack signals (Nos. 28–29) besides Nelson's code, and whether the Sirius's three guns at 9.35 p.m. meant 'standing west'. James has the enemy standing north-west, the French reports S to SSW (a-h3.md, R18).

Night distances and positions. The Euryalus's midnight bearing of the enemy is SE by S in NRS II 149 and SE by E in Nicolas VII 134 n. The Sirius was 4 miles off at midnight (NRS II 313) or 6 at 11.30 (Nicolas). The enemy's midnight position is interpolated, and Desbrière's British midnight position cannot be reconciled with the dawn positions (a-h2c.md, H2-32i).

The British wear lights (two at the ensign staff, one at the bowsprit end) and the form of No. 31 (three guns and two lights, or a square of four lanterns) come from the 1799 book; no log of that night records them. The six guns the Sirius heard at 9.35 p.m. may be No. 31 repeated by two flagships, an inference only (a-h3.md, R16, R25).
All ranges are estimates: flag colours readable at about 4–11 nm, lanterns at 1–3 nm, blue lights at 5–14 nm (a-h3.md, R21–R22).
Flag colours. The 1804 values of the numeral flags (Perrin's Plate XIII) were not transcribed, and which half of Popham's telegraph flag was red is disputed (a-h3.md, R28).
Clocks and light. If the Victory's clock ran about 45 minutes slow on the 19th (an inference in a-h3.md, R10), her 9.30 was about 10.15 local time, with the sun about 37° up rather than 32°.
keySources: T. Sturges Jackson (ed.), Logs of the Great Sea Fights 1794–1805, vol. II (Navy Records Society, 1900). It gave the Euryalus's log (pp. 145–150) and signal log (pp. 160–168); the Naiad, Phoebe (incl. No. 370 'with two guns' on 23 Oct, p. 308), Sirius, Pickle, Mars, Colossus, Leviathan, Orion and Agamemnon logs; and Browne's and Walker's letters, all by civil date. Euryalus p. 145: https://archive.org/details/logsofgreatseaf02jack/page/n162/mode/1up ; signal log p. 160: https://archive.org/details/logsofgreatseaf02jack/page/n177/mode/1up ; Phoebe p. 306: https://archive.org/details/logsofgreatseaf02jack/page/n323/mode/1up ; Sirius p. 312: https://archive.org/details/logsofgreatseaf02jack/page/n329/mode/1up

N. H. Nicolas (ed.), The Dispatches and Letters of Lord Nelson, vol. VII (1846). It gave the orders of 4 and 10 October (pp. 70–73, 109–111), Blackwood's letter of 19 October (p. 131 n.), the frigates' logs for 20 October (p. 134 n.) and the memorandum and night code of 20 October (p. 136): https://archive.org/details/dispatchesletter07nelsuoft/page/n171/mode/1up

G. Hudson (ed.), Nelson's Last Diary (1917), pp. 21–24. It gave the manuscript's readings: the 14 October chain, 'ESE by compass, distance 16 leagues' on 19 October, and 'At 5 o'clock' for the Naiad's signal and the night wears on 20 October: https://archive.org/details/nelsonslastdiary00nelsuoft/page/n28/mode/1up

W. Beatty, Authentic Narrative of the Death of Lord Nelson (1807). It gave the cordon (p. 6), the 9.30 signal, the chase with two guns and the light SSW airs (p. 7), the night signals (pp. 9–10), the 2 a.m. variant (p. 11) and the diary in the appendix (pp. 96–99): https://archive.org/details/b22036611_0001/page/n16/mode/1up

J. S. Corbett, The Campaign of Trafalgar (1910). It gave Popham's code (pp. 298–301); the relay, the chase signal, the Téméraire's courses and the Victory's noon position (p. 333 and n. 1); the clock offset (p. 339 n. 2); and No. 31, the Victory's blue lights and the 'hourly' reports (p. 340). Page image of p. 333 checked: https://archive.org/details/campaignoftrafal00corb/page/n368/mode/1up

W. P. Cumby, letter to his son, The Nineteenth Century 46 (November 1899), pp. 718–719. It gave the Mars hull-down, her distant signal of a flag, a ball and a pendant, and the Victory answering her: https://archive.org/details/sim_twentieth-century_1899-11_46_273/page/n32/mode/1up

Admiralty, Night Signals and Instructions for the Conduct of Ships of War (1799). It gave the night numerals (pp. 3–5), repeating and answering (pp. 7–11), No. 31 and its wear lights (p. 16), the lantern figures (pp. 25–26) and the instructions for watching an enemy (pp. 39–41): https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_night-signals-and-instru_1799/page/n16/mode/1up

H. Popham, Telegraphic Signals; or Marine Vocabulary (1803), p. 6. It gave the telegraph flag and the rule to keep a signal flying until it is repeated to the commander-in-chief: https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_qxZEAAAAYAAJ/page/n10/mode/1up

Admiralty, Signal-Book for the Ships of War (1796). It gave guns with day signals, two guns for a general chase, and the repeating of a private ship's signals: https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_signal-book-for-the-ship_1796
W. G. Perrin, British Flags (1922). It gave the 1799 Signal Book, the 1803–04 change of flag values and the manuscript additions: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/46370

E. Fraser, The Enemy at Trafalgar (1906). It gave the French and Spanish accounts of the night (pp. 88–96), Gravina's flagship timing British guns by flash and report (p. 94), and the Defence's hidden lights and the lit enemy line (p. 95): https://archive.org/details/enemyattrafalgar00frasuoft/page/n125/mode/1up

É. Desbrière, La campagne maritime de 1805: Trafalgar (1907), annexes. It gave Prigny (p. 139), the Scipion's feux bleus, amorces and rockets (p. 154), the Cornélie (p. 159) and the Bucentaure's SSW course (p. 178): https://archive.org/details/la-campagne-maritime-de-1805/page/n427/mode/1up

W. James, The Naval History of Great Britain, vol. III (1886 ed.), pp. 388–390. It gave the WSW reading, the enemy standing north-west and the 8.40 p.m. wear: https://archive.org/details/navalhistoryofgr03jameuoft/page/n406/mode/1up
W. H. Smyth, The Sailor's Word-Book (1867). It gave the false fire and the blue light, and the false fire's burn of half a minute to several minutes: https://archive.org/details/smythsailorswordbook

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 2nd ed. (1778), 'Pyrotechny'. It gave signal rockets and blue-burning compositions of sulphur and saltpetre: https://jimclifford.ca/early_encyclopedia_britannica/articles/1778/eb_2nd_1778_011922.html

J. K. Laughton, 'Colomb, Philip Howard', Dictionary of National Biography, 1901 supplement. It gave the adoption of flashing signals in 1867: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Dictionary_of_National_Biography,_1901_supplement/Colomb,_Philip_Howard

EMODnet Bathymetry, depth sample service. It gave modern depths at every chain position, all in open water at about 30–550 m (not 1805 soundings): https://rest.emodnet-bathymetry.eu/depth_sample?geom=POINT(-6.364%2036.475)
ownerQuestions: The beat 4 caption says 'a chain of frigates', but the outer links were ships of the line (Defence, Colossus, Mars). Should it read 'linked to the coast by a chain of frigates and ships of the line', or 'by a chain of ships'? Recommended.

At the last link the Mars switched to a colour-blind distant signal (a flag, a ball and a pendant at three mastheads) because she was hull-down from the fleet. It rests on one eyewitness writing years later (Cumby). Should it be the closing moment of the relay, or should every link keep to coloured flags?

Some details come only from the 1799 rule books, not from the logs of those days: hoists held along the chain until the Victory's answer runs back, and three lights on every British ship during the night wears. Should the scene show these by-the-book details, or only what the logs record?

briefRows.brief: Concept: the army at Boulogne shown as 'rows of tiny tents'
briefRows.sources: The camps were hutted. From autumn 1803 the troops lived in wooden huts (baraques) built for the winter, in rows by regiment: one division of Soult's corps had 748 in May–June 1804, and the huts excavated at Étaples had tiled roofs and glazed windows. Tents were campaign kit, sent from Metz to Strasbourg in August 1805 (Desbrière, Projets III 206–207, 432–433; Corr. XI No. 9137; Fondation Napoléon newsletter 410)
briefRows.scene: Rows of small huts along camp streets: Soult's two camps on the plateaus either side of the Liane (the right one by the Tour d'Ordre, with Napoleon's hut), Lannes at Wimereux, Davout at Ambleteuse, Ney at Étaples and Montreuil

briefRows.brief: Beat 1 caption: 'a flotilla of invasion barges'; concept: 'the invasion flotilla in the harbour'
briefRows.sources: Rigged gun craft, not barges: ship-rigged three-masted prames, brig-rigged chaloupes canonnières, lug-rigged bateaux canonniers and péniches, with fishing and merchant craft as transports. On 20 July 1805 Boulogne held 1,104 (578 armed, 526 transports) of 2,293 in seven ports. They lay in the tidal basin of the Liane, and lines of them were moored in the road outside the pier (88 in July 1804, about 150 in October 1804) (Desbrière, Projets III 90; James III 216–217, 227, 232, 325)
briefRows.scene: Instanced rigged craft: a few prames, many brigs and luggers. The caption may keep 'invasion barges' or say 'invasion craft'. Natural Earth makes the Liane basin land, so the visible flotilla lies in the road off the harbour mouth
briefRows.confidence: high for the designs and the count; medium as built; low for the layout in August 1805

briefRows.brief: History: 'Late August 1805: Napoleon abandons the invasion'; beat 3 caption: 'Napoleon gives up on England'
briefRows.sources: He put it off 'à une autre année' (23 August, Corr. XI No. 9120). He left nineteen battalions and the flotilla at Boulogne as a standing threat, and on 13 September planned to keep 500 craft and 80,000 men there. He decided on 23–26 August, before he knew Villeneuve was in Cádiz (by 31 August at the latest)
briefRows.scene: The caption may stand; 'puts off' is nearer his words. It may put Cádiz before the turn east, but must not suggest that the news caused the turn

briefRows.brief: History: 'On 20 October an Austrian army under Mack surrenders at Ulm'; beat 5 caption
briefRows.sources: The capitulation was signed on 17 October (at noon by Alombert and Colin, 2 p.m. by the Austrian eyewitness). On 20 October, from 2 p.m., the garrison marched out and laid down its arms before Napoleon: about 25,000 men (Alombert and Colin III/1 225–229; 7th and 8th Bulletins)
briefRows.scene: 20 October 1805 on the date line and in the cut-away. 'Lays down its arms' is exact; 'surrenders' is defensible. Never 19 October

briefRows.brief: Beat 4 caption: 'linked to the coast by a chain of frigates'
briefRows.sources: Frigates (Euryalus, Sirius, Phoebe, Naiad) only at the Cádiz end. The chain itself was ships of the line: Mars, Defence and Colossus from 4 October; Defence, Agamemnon, Colossus and Mars from 14 October (Nicolas VII 70–73, 122; Beatty 1825, p. 7; Codrington 1873, I 57)
briefRows.scene: Same length: '…linked to the coast by a chain of warships.' ('a chain of warships' has 19 characters, like 'a chain of frigates'). Shorter: '…by a chain of ships.' On the chart: frigates inshore, ships of the line in the chain

briefRows.brief: Beat 4: 'the combined fleet in the harbour'
briefRows.sources: From 9–10 October the fleet lay in the roadstead at the harbour mouth, out of range of the city's guns, moored with springs and two anchors (NW and SE); a few ships stayed deeper in at the Puntal–Matagorda narrows until 19 October. 33 of the line were ready (18 French, 15 Spanish), with 5 frigates and 2 brigs; Terrible and San Fulgencio were laid up (research/scene-02/a-h2c.md, H2-36c–e, H2-40a)
briefRows.scene: 33 ship glyphs at anchor in open water north-east of the entrance shoals, off the reef and the shore (see 'Positions on the chart'), heads about 294° true; a few at the narrows until the 19th
briefRows.confidence: medium for the description, low for the coordinates

fleetRows.shipsOfTheLine: None. Craft: 1,104 at Boulogne (578 prames and gun craft, 526 transports) of 2,293 in the seven ports (1,339 armed, 954 transports). Other counts are right for their own dates: 1,301 built in 1803–04 (Desbrière), 2,054 in spring 1805 (embarkation return)
fleetRows.others: Instanced rigged craft, not ship glyphs: a few prames, many brigs and luggers
fleetRows.sources: James III 217, 325; Clowes V 62; Desbrière, Projets III 90, IV 433

fleetRows.stage: Collingwood off Cádiz before Nelson came
fleetRows.shipsOfTheLine: 26, after Calder joined with 18 on 30 August
fleetRows.others: An inshore squadron under Louis; Lauriston saw 5 of the line and 2 frigates at 3 leagues and 17 more at 6 leagues on 3 September
fleetRows.sources: Desbrière 1907, pp. 143–145; James III 379

fleetRows.shipsOfTheLine: 29 counting Victory, Ajax and Thunderer: 23 in the main body and 6 inshore under Louis (Victory's log and signal log; Nelson to Acton, 30 September; Mahan; ship-by-ship tally). James and Beatty: 27 (22 offshore + 5 inshore)
fleetRows.others: Few frigates: only 3 with the fleet on 4 October; Euryalus and Hydra off the port from 29 September
fleetRows.sources: Nicolas VII 53 n., 54; Desbrière 1907, pp. 143–145; James III 379; Beatty 1825, p. 3; research/scene-02/a-h2b.md, H2-16
fleetRows.confidence: high for 29 under his command; medium for all 29 in company

fleetRows.shipsOfTheLine: 5 leave (Queen 98, Canopus 80, Spencer 74, Tigre 74, Zealous 74; Nelson called it six). 23 left with Nelson by 5 October, Leviathan being away at Gibraltar until the 8th. Four of Louis's ships briefly rejoined on 4 or 5 October and left again
fleetRows.others: With Louis: the frigate Endymion and five merchantmen; Zealous and Endymion went on to Gibraltar
fleetRows.sources: Nicolas VII 63, 75; Hubback 1906, pp. 148–149; James III 380

fleetRows.shipsOfTheLine: 28 by the ship-by-ship tally (23 → 24 on 7 Oct → 26 on 8 Oct → 27 on 10 Oct → 28 on 13 Oct forenoon → 27 that evening → 28 with Africa). James and Clowes give 29, which needs Africa to have joined before Prince of Wales sailed
fleetRows.others: Never show 29 in mid-October
fleetRows.sources: Nicolas VII 75–121; James III 383; Clowes V 128; research/scene-02/a-h2b.md, H2-19a

fleetRows.stage: Off Cádiz, from Donegal's departure through the battle
fleetRows.others: Frigates Euryalus, Naiad, Phoebe, Sirius; schooner Pickle; cutter Entreprenante; the brig Weazle was sent to Gibraltar on 19 October
fleetRows.sources: Nicolas VII 130; James III 383–384; Conqueror's log (NRS II)

fleetRows.shipsOfTheLine: 5 of the line with the Malta convoy (Austen; a telegraph report reaching Villeneuve said 4), some 200 miles east of the Strait at dawn on 20 October; Donegal at Gibraltar
fleetRows.others: 3 frigates with Louis (Austen). Out of the Gulf frame
fleetRows.sources: Hubback 1906, pp. 152–153; Corbett 1910, pp. 332, 335

fleetRows.stage: The combined fleet in Cádiz before the sortie

openDoubts: British strength at Nelson's arrival, 28 September: 29 of the line (Victory's log and signal log; Nelson to Acton, 30 September; Mahan; ship tally) or 27 (James III 379; Beatty p. 3). All 29 were in company only if Leviathan had not yet gone to Gibraltar.
The October peak: 28 by the ship-by-ship tally, or 29 (James III 383; Clowes V 128), which needs Africa to have joined before Prince of Wales sailed on the evening of 13 October.

Louis's departure and return: sailed the evening of 2 October (Austen; Nelson; the log's nautical 'October 3rd') or on 3 October (Desbrière p. 148); rejoined on 4 October (Beatty) or the morning of the 5th (Austen).
When the orders of 14 September reached Cádiz: 27 September (Decrès's report) or 28 September (Desbrière p. 136; James; Clowes; Corbett: as Nelson appeared off Cape St Vincent).

Rosily: in Madrid in the night of 10–11 October (Beurnonville; Desbrière p. 128 has the 10th; Corbett's 12 October is his letter's date); at Cádiz on 23 October (expected, Beurnonville) or 25 October (Fraser; his first letter). Villeneuve heard he was in Madrid on 18 October (his own letter; Desbrière, Corbett) or about 15–16 October (Fraser p. 63).
Magon's planned night sortie of 18 October: four French and three Spanish of the line and the Hermione (Villeneuve's letter, Desbrière annexes 101; Corbett) or three ships (Desbrière p. 141).

Ships of the line out on 19 October: seven (Philibert, the Montañés, Desbrière) against 6–7 (Rhin), 7–8 (Fougueux), eight French (Observateur), four at 4.30 p.m. (Thémis), nine (Prigny, from memory) and twelve (James, Nicolas, from the Euryalus's count of all sail).

When the whole fleet was out on 20 October: about 8–8.30 a.m. (Observateur, Montañés, Fougueux), about 11 (Desbrière p. 163) or nearly noon (Corbett p. 337). The afternoon wear: between 1 and 3 p.m. (Desbrière), 3.30 (Sirius) or about 4 (Corbett, Prigny); three columns (Prigny, Fougueux, Desbrière) or five (James; Nicolas, citing the Spanish official report).

The anchorage: no source fixes the ships' places. The layout rests on Escaño ('fuera del tiro de la plaza'), the French 'entre les Porques et le Diamant', Nelson's 'harbour's mouth', a-h2c's reading of modern depths, and Faden's 1797 plan, which shows the Spanish moorings of 1797, not those of 1805. How many ships stayed in the narrows is not recorded, and the sheet does not say whether its soundings are fathoms or Spanish brazas.
Defence's latitude on 19 October: on Cádiz's parallel by the order of 4 October and a-h2c (36°32′ N), or about 10 nm south of it by the Euryalus's bearing 'west' (a-h2b, H2-37f: 36°19′–25′ N).

The British midnight position on 20–21 October (about 20 miles SW of Cádiz, Desbrière p. 178) cannot be joined to the dawn position to better than 5–15 nm. At dawn the combined fleet lay 10–12 nm from the coast by British reckoning and 18–24 nm by French (Dumanoir, Scipion).

Ulm: about 23,000 (the Austrian eyewitness), 25,365 (Alombert and Colin), 27,000 (7th Bulletin) or 30,000 (8th Bulletin) laid down their arms; the capitulation was signed at noon (Alombert and Colin) or at 2 p.m. (the eyewitness). Napoleon was at Donauwörth on 7 October in the afternoon (Schuermans) or the morning (Maude).

Napoleon left Boulogne on 2 September (Corr. XI No. 9177; Desbrière) or on 4 September (James III 332). The second divisions marched on 30 August (Berthier's order) or on 29 August ('demain' in Napoleon's letter of the 28th).
Gun counts: Santísima Trinidad 130 (Nicolas VII 130), 136 (scene 1 notes) or 140 (Desbrière p. 134); Prince of Wales 98 (James, Clowes) or 90 (Desbrière, Mahan).
Boulogne's flotilla in August 1805: the lines moored in the road are documented for 1804 (James III 217, 227, 232) and intended after Napoleon left (III 332); their layout in August 1805 is not.
Not consulted first-hand: Tofiño's own 1789 plan (only Faden's English copy of 1797), Victory's master's log for 1–21 October (ADM 52), the Spanish official report in full.

rulings.point: Which ocean form to set: ATLANTIC OCEAN (v-h4) or Faden's ATLANTIC or WESTERN OCEAN (h4's preference for the ocean view); v-h4's reading of Cary 1805
rulings.finalStatement: Set ATLANTIC OCEAN. Cary's West India Isles (1803) and Arrowsmith's West Indies chart (1803) engrave exactly that, Heather (1800) and Cary's Europe (1804) engrave THE ATLANTIC OCEAN, and it is the usual name in print (Malham 237 against 7 for 'Western Ocean'; Brookes 1807 55 against 0). ATLANTIC or WESTERN OCEAN (Faden 1807 and Laurie & Whittle 1794, both read; Heather's chart titles of about 1806) is equally period and is the title of the chart the scene imitates. It stays an option only if the lettering sets it over three lines with a small 'or'. Cary 1801 reverses it: WESTERN OR ATLANTIC OCEAN. Correction to v-h4: Cary's Africa (1805) engraves NORTH PACIFIC OCEAN off West Africa, an engraver's slip, not NORTH ATLANTIC OCEAN.

rulings.point: 'The Channel' (on the chart now), 'English Channel' (h4's best) or 'British Channel' (v-h4: disputed)
rulings.finalStatement: Set English Channel. Faden 1807 engraves ENGLISH CHANNEL in spaced roman capitals (read). Heather's catalogue of about 1806 sells 'The English Channel on three Sheets', and Norie 1805, Malham 1795 (123 against 7) and Brookes 1807 use 'English Channel'. Cary's Europe (1804) engraves BRITISH CHANNEL (read), and Heather also sold Directions for the British Channel. Laurie & Whittle 1794 has THE CHANNEL (read), and sailors wrote 'the Channel' (some 33 times in Nelson vols. 6–7). All three are period forms; English Channel has the most charts and chart titles of 1800–1807 behind it, matches the model chart and is unambiguous today.

rulings.point: h4: no prose of 1805 uses it, 0 hits in Brookes; v-h4: Brookes and other gazetteers use it
rulings.finalStatement: The name is period-correct. On English charts it appears only on Heather's Coast of Portugal of 3 April 1800, as GULF OF CADIZ in open roman capitals slanting from off the Algarve towards Cadiz (read, imprint read). Faden 1807, Cary 1801, Cary 1804 and Heather's Strait plate of c. 1809 leave the water unnamed. In print it was a geographers' name: Brookes 1807 puts Alcoutim, Faro and Tavira on 'the gulf of Cadiz' (read). Per v-h4 the Brookes editions of 1795–1801, Walker, Cruttwell, Pinkerton and the Britannica of 1810 use it too. Naval writing never does: 0 in Nelson, the logs, the Naval Chronicle 14 and Malham. Sailors said 'off Cadiz'. Spell it Gulf, as Heather's chart and Brookes do; 'Gulph' now looks like a misprint.

rulings.point: How much water the name covers
rulings.finalStatement: There are two versions. (1) The whole bight from the Algarve to Cadiz: Heather 1800 places the name in that open water, and the gazetteers put Faro, Tavira, Ayamonte and the Guadiana mouth on the gulf. (2) Mostly the bay: Tuckey (1815) says the curve from Cape St Mary to Cape Trafalgar is 'sometimes called the Gulf of Cadiz', but that the name was more usually kept for the Bay of Cadiz. The chart follows version 1, as its only period chart does; the label at 36.22 N, 7.0 W lies in that water.

rulings.point: h4: 'Streights' out of fashion by 1800; v-h4: it lingered in official texts
rulings.finalStatement: Set Straits of Gibraltar (unchanged). Heather 1800 and Heather c. 1809 (large open roman capitals) engrave STRAITS OF GIBRALTAR, as does Cary 1801 (italic capitals; all read). Cary 1804 abbreviates it STR. OF GIBRALTAR (read). Malham has 'Straits of Gibraltar' 22 times and 'Streights' never. v-h4 is right that 'Streights' survived in official documents of 1800–1807, but charts and naval writing had dropped it. Faden's 1806 chart title has the singular 'Strait' (per h4).

rulings.point: The stopless 'C. St Vincent' on the chart now
rulings.finalStatement: Set C. St. Vincent (the checker agrees). The engravers wrote S with a raised t and a stop: Faden 1807 has 'C. Sᵗ. Vincent' in upright roman, and Heather 1800 has CAPE Sᵀ. VINCENT (both read; Cary 1801 and 1805 per v-h4). Printed English of 1805 always has the stop: 'Cape St. Vincent' in Nelson (30 and 35 hits, none stopless, per both notes) and in Malham (20). The stopless 'St' is a later British habit. The same rule applies to every St., Sta., Pt. and Mt. on the chart.

rulings.point: v-h4's variant 'Tangiers' (Cary 1804)
rulings.finalStatement: Set Tangier, as on Faden 1807, Heather 1800, Heather c. 1809 (TANGIER, Old Tangier, Tangier Bay, read) and Cary 1801 (v-h4). Nelson has 'Tangier' 9 times and 'Tangiers' once, Malham 17 to 0 and Brookes 3 to 0. Cary's Europe (1804) engraves 'Tangiers' (read), a variant.

rulings.point: 'Western Islands' (on the chart now; v-h4 confirmed) against h4's 'Azores or Western Isles'
rulings.finalStatement: Set Azores or Western Islands. v-h4 is right that 'Western Islands' alone was an engraved name: Arrowsmith's Africa (1802) letters WESTERN ISLANDS beside St. Miguel and St. Mary, and Cary's Africa (1805) has WESTERN Iˢ (both read). Nelson, Norie and Malham call the group the Western Islands, and Nelson's uses all mean the Azores. h4 is right that a modern visitor cannot find the Azores under that name, and the story needs them: Nelson passed through the group north of São Miguel on 8–9 July. 'Western Isles' is today the official name of the Outer Hebrides. The double name is period-exact: Laurie & Whittle 1794 engraves AZORES or WESTERN ISLANDS (read), and Heather's catalogue of about 1806 sells a chart of 'The Azores, or Western Islands'. Faden 1807 has AZORES OR WESTERN ISLES (read). 'Islands' matches Nelson, Norie, Heather and the chart's own 'Canary Islands'.

rulings.point: h4's table sets 'Canary Isles'; v-h4 keeps 'Canary Islands'
rulings.finalStatement: Keep Canary Islands. Arrowsmith's Africa (1802) engraves CANARY ISLANDS (read), as does Laurie & Whittle 1794 (h4). Heather's catalogue sells 'Madeira and the Canary Islands', and Nelson, Malham (14 to 0) and Brookes (3 to 0) write 'Canary Islands'. CANARY ISLES on Faden 1807 and Cary 1805 (both read) is equally period, but the charts of the decade disagree, so the usage of 1805 decides.

rulings.point: v-h4: a regional label, not a water
rulings.finalStatement: West Indies is right and was the universal word (Malham 312; Nelson 84 by v-h4's count). No chart read letters it in the map body. Faden 1807 uses it in his track legend, 'Track of H.M.S. Victory to the West Indies 1805' (read), and it is in chart titles: Arrowsmith 1803 (read), Cary's West India Isles 1803, Heather's catalogue. Set it as a regional label in Baskervville roman (the island role), never in the italic of waters; the gazetteer already does this. The engraved name of the arc is CARIBBEE ISLANDS (Faden 1807, Cary 1803, Arrowsmith 1803, all read).

rulings.point: 'Martinico' (on the chart now) against 'Martinique'
rulings.finalStatement: Set Martinique. English sources of 1794–1807 are split, and not along the line v-h4 drew. Martinique: Faden 1807 (read), Cary's West India Isles 1803 (MARTINIQUE, read), the Naval Chronicle of 1805 (12 to 2) and Norie's 1805 tables of positions. Martinico: Nelson's own letters (12 in vols. 6–7, e.g. 'they landed 1000 sick when they arrived at Martinico'), Arrowsmith's West Indies chart of 1803 (MARTINICO, with Little Martinico; read), Laurie & Whittle 1794 (read), Malham 1795 (39 to 6) and Brookes 1807 (5 to 0). Where the charts disagree, the modern visitor decides: Martinique is the form of the chart the scene imitates and of the brief and site prose, while Martinico reads as another place or a slip. Nelson's word belongs in the history notes.

rulings.point: h4: 'Cape Roca' was not English; v-h4: Cary 1801 letters 'C. of Roca'
rulings.finalStatement: Set Rock of Lisbon: Faden 1807 (read), Heather 1800 (ROCK OF LISBON, read), Laurie & Whittle 1794; Nelson dates a letter 'Victory, off the Rock of Lisbon' on 25 September 1805, and Malham has 6 hits. v-h4 is right that h4's flag was too strong: Cary 1801 engraves 'C. of Roca' (read). Sailors also called the cape Cape Roxent (Malham 4; Tuckey 1815).

rulings.point: Algeziras, Algesiras or Algeciras
rulings.finalStatement: Set Algeziras, the form of the English charts of 1800–1801: Heather 1800 (ALGEZIRAS BAY, Algeziras I.) and Cary 1801 (Algeziras, read). The Naval Chronicle 1805 has 3 against 2 'Algesiras', and Malham has 3. Nelson's letters prefer Algesiras (26 to 7). Algeciras, today's spelling, is on Heather's Strait plate after Tofiño of c. 1809 (read) and once in the logs.

rulings.point: Gulf of Lion (h4) or Gulf of Lyons (v-h4)
rulings.finalStatement: Set Gulf of Lyons: Cary 1801 (GULF of LYONS) and Cary 1804 (GULF OF LYONS), both read, in italic capitals. Nelson writes 'Gulf of Lyons' in his own orders and letters (5 in vol. 6, e.g. his intention to get into the Gulf of Lyons), as do Malham (7) and Brookes (1). There are no hits for 'Gulf of Lion'; that form belongs to older charts (La Rochette 1780; Laurie & Whittle 1794, per h4).

rulings.point: Rochefort or Rochfort
rulings.finalStatement: Set Rochefort: Faden 1807 (read), the Naval Chronicle 1805 (13 to 2), and Nicolas's vol. 7, mostly letters of August–October 1805 (13 to 0). Rochfort is on Cary 1804 (read), in vol. 6, letters of 1804–05 (5 to 1), and in Malham (4).

rulings.point: Douro or Duero
rulings.finalStatement: Set Douro for the river at Oporto, which is all the chart can show from the sea: Cary's Portugal 1801 (per h4), Malham and Brookes. Cary's Europe 1804 engraves 'R. Duero' at the mouth (read), the Spanish name of the whole river.

rulings.point: C. St. Mary, C. St. Maria, C. Sta. Maria or C. S. Mary
rulings.finalStatement: Set C. St. Mary, the English form: Nelson's 'Cape St. Mary' (19), the logs (3), the Naval Chronicle (4) and Malham (27). Faden 1807 engraves 'C. S. Mary' (read). The Iberian forms are on the coastal plates: 'C. Sᵗ Maria' (Heather 1800) and 'C. Sᵗᵃ Maria' (Cary 1801, read).

rulings.point: Guadalquiver (h4) or Guadalquivir (Cary 1801)
rulings.finalStatement: Set Guadalquivir. The commoner English form of 1795–1807 was Guadalquiver: Faden 1807 (read), Heather 1800 (GUADALQUIVER RIVER), Knight c. 1795, Malham (11 to 0) and Brookes 1807 (6 to 0). But the charts disagree: Cary 1801 engraves 'R. Guadalquivir' (read), as La Rochette/Faden did in 1780. Today '-quiver' reads as a misprint, so the chart takes the period form that does not.

rulings.point: Leave unlettered (h4) or GREAT DESERT OF ZAARA (v-h4)
rulings.finalStatement: Leave it unlettered: sea charts did not name the interior. v-h4 is right that a period form exists: Cary 1805 engraves GREAT DESERT OF ZAARA (read). Arrowsmith 1802 engraves SAARA OR GREAT DESERT (read), and Brookes 1807 writes Zahara (10 hits, all the desert). If a later scene letters it, set Saara or Great Desert, the period form closest to today's name.

rulings.point: h4's 'Cape Verd Isles' (not checked by v-h4; new evidence)
rulings.finalStatement: Set Cape Verde Islands. The charts of the decade disagree: Arrowsmith's Africa (1802) engraves CAPE VERDE ISLANDS and 'Cape Verde' (read), Faden 1807 and Cary 1805 have CAPE VERD ISLES (read), and Laurie & Whittle 1794 CAPE VERD ISLANDS (h4). The navigation books write 'Cape Verd' (Norie, Moore). 'Verd' looks like a slip today.

rulings.point: h4: huge spaced roman capitals, open or hatched, broken over lines; v-h4: confirmed in the core, the details are Faden's
rulings.finalStatement: Oceans were lettered in the largest spaced roman capitals on every chart read. Open, outline or hatched letters are Faden's and Laurie & Whittle's habit; Cary, Arrowsmith and Heather 1800 engrave plain solid roman, and shaded open capitals appear on Heather's c. 1809 plate for the Strait. The chart's solid Bodoni Moda capitals, widely tracked, are period. Breaking the name over lines or along a curve is optional.

rulings.id: Lettering: seas, the Channel, gulfs, straits
rulings.point: h4: spaced roman capitals, italic only for small waters; v-h4: Cary sets gulfs and straits in spaced italic capitals
rulings.finalStatement: The big waters were spaced capitals on every chart read. Seas and the Channel were roman (Faden 1807, Cary 1801 and 1804, Heather 1800). Gulfs and straits were roman on Heather (GULF OF CADIZ, STRAITS OF GIBRALTAR) and italic capitals on Cary (GULF OF LYONS, STR. OF GIBRALTAR, STRAITS of GIBRALTAR; read). Small waters (roads, bays) were italic. The chart's convention, seas in spaced italic capitals and other waters in italic upper and lower case, simplifies this within the brief; the italic itself is period.

rulings.point: h4: spaced italic capitals on an arc; v-h4: Faden's habit, not a rule
rulings.finalStatement: Groups were spaced capitals, roman or italic by engraver. Roman: Cary 1805 MADEIRA ISLES and CANARY ISLES; CARIBBEE ISLANDS on Faden, Cary 1803 and Arrowsmith 1803; Arrowsmith 1802 CANARY ISLANDS and WESTERN ISLANDS. Italic: Faden 1807 AZORES OR WESTERN ISLES, MADEIRA ISLES and CANARY ISLES; Laurie & Whittle 1794 AZORES or WESTERN ISLANDS (all read). Single islands were roman upper and lower case. The chart's Baskervville roman upper and lower case for both is period in face.

rulings.point: v-h4: confirmed, scale-dependent
rulings.finalStatement: Capitals were set in capitals (Faden 1807 MADRID, PARIS, LONDON; Cary 1804 LONDON, PARIS) and ports in roman upper and lower case on small-scale charts. On larger scales big ports go into capitals too (Cary 1801 CADIZ, LISBON, GIBRALTAR; Heather 1800 CADIZ). The chart's roman upper and lower case beside a ring, with the dotted ring and a larger cap for capitals, stands.

rulings.point: v-h4: partly confirmed (S. also occurs; large-scale charts spell 'Cape'; the upright/italic split is not general)
rulings.finalStatement: 'C.' with a stop is the small-scale form on every chart read. 'Cape' is spelled out only on large-scale coastal plates (Heather 1800 CAPE Sᵀ. VINCENT; Heather c. 1809 Cape Trafalgar, CAPE SPARTEL, Cape Plata). Faden's split, landfall capes upright and lesser capes italic, is his habit: Cary 1804 sets C. Trafalgar and C. Espartel both italic (read). A plain 'S.' also occurs (Faden 'C. S. Mary'; Cary 1803 'S. Vincent'). The chart sets every cape in italic as 'C. Name' at every zoom and writes saints 'St.'.

rulings.point: h4: 6.5 : 2.8 : 1.4 : 1.2 : 1 (ocean : country : capital : port : minor); v-h4: unverifiable, Cary's oceans much less dominant
rulings.finalStatement: The ratios were measured on Faden 1807 (t4) and hold for that chart. v-h4 is right about Cary: on Europe 1804 the ocean letters are scarcely larger than the country names. The chart's hierarchy belongs to decisions.md and a-t4.md and is not changed by this ruling.

conventions.statement: Letter the form the English charts of 1800–1807 engraved, Faden's chart of 1807 first. Break ties with 1805 naval usage (Nelson, logs, Naval Chronicle, Norie, Malham). Where the charts disagree, take the form a modern visitor will not misread as a misprint or another place (Martinique, Guadalquivir, Cape Verde Islands, the Azores in the double name). Where they agree on a form that looks odd today (Barbadoes, Bourdeaux, Guadaloupe, Carthagena, Ivica), keep it and record it.
Bodoni Moda capitals, widely spaced, solid as Cary and Arrowsmith engraved them (Faden's open letters are his habit). One line, or broken over lines along the ocean; no article.
Baskervville italic capitals, spaced, as the brief allows. Period plates set seas in spaced roman capitals.
Baskervville italic, upper and lower case. Period plates set the big ones in spaced capitals, roman (Faden, Heather) or italic (Cary), and small waters in italic.

'C.' with a full stop and the name, italic, at every zoom. 'Cape' was spelled out only on large-scale coastal plates. Points as 'Pt.', or spelled out where the period spelled them (Europa Point, Rock of Lisbon).
The engraved superior letters are typeset with a full stop: St. (Sᵗ), Sta. (Sᵗᵃ), Pt. (Pᵗ), Mt. (Mᵗ), Is. (Iˢ, several islands), I. for one island. Never the stopless modern 'St'.
None on the chart: Cadiz, Malaga, Leon, Tetuan, Sicie, Rhone. English charts and prose of 1805 used no accents; the site's own prose may keep modern accents.
Baskervville roman, upper and lower case, beside a ring. Capitals (Lisbon, Madrid, Paris, London, Vienna) take the dotted ring and a larger cap; the period plates set them in capitals.
Baskervville roman, upper and lower case. Period plates used spaced capitals, mostly roman, sometimes italic.

Baskervville roman, upper and lower case, on the sea. Period plates set groups in spaced capitals, roman (Cary, Arrowsmith) or italic (Faden, Laurie & Whittle), and single islands in roman upper and lower case.
Set with a lower-case 'or' ('Azores or Western Islands'), as the plates set a small 'or' between capitals. They may break over two lines.
Drop 'The' on labels ('Atlantic Ocean', 'English Channel'), as Faden 1807, Cary 1803 and Arrowsmith 1803 did; Heather 1800 and Cary 1804 have it.
Italic, upper and lower case, without 'R.' unless needed. Period plates wrote 'Tagus R.' or 'R. Tagus', and spaced capitals along big lower courses.
Named ranges are an atlas convention (Cary, Arrowsmith); sea charts named only coastal heights. Set them in upper and lower case.
Never copied: 'C. Trafalagar' and 'Teutan' (Cary 1801); NORTH PACIFIC OCEAN off West Africa (Cary 1805).

doubts: Martinique or Martinico: the chart letters Martinique, as Faden's chart of Nelson's track (1807), Cary's West India map (1803), the Naval Chronicle of 1805 and Norie's 1805 tables do. Nelson's own letters, Arrowsmith's West Indies chart (1803), Laurie & Whittle (1794), Malham (1795) and Brookes (1807) write Martinico.

The Channel: the chart letters English Channel (Faden 1807; Heather's chart titles of about 1806; Norie 1805; Malham). Cary's Europe (1804) engraves BRITISH CHANNEL, Laurie & Whittle's Atlantic (1794) THE CHANNEL, and Nelson and his officers simply wrote 'the Channel'.

The Azores: the chart letters Azores or Western Islands, as Laurie & Whittle (1794) and a Heather chart title of about 1806 do. Faden (1807) has Azores or Western Isles; Arrowsmith (1802), Cary (1805), Nelson and Norie call them simply the Western Islands.
Canary Islands or Isles: Canary Islands on Arrowsmith 1802 and Laurie & Whittle 1794, in Heather's chart titles and in Nelson, Malham and Brookes. Canary Isles on Faden 1807 and Cary 1805.

The ocean: ATLANTIC OCEAN on Cary 1803 and Arrowsmith 1803, THE ATLANTIC OCEAN on Heather 1800 and Cary 1804, and the usual name in print. The ocean charts of Laurie & Whittle (1794) and Faden (1807) and Heather's chart titles say Atlantic or Western Ocean; Cary's Spain (1801) says Western or Atlantic Ocean.

Gulf of Cadiz: on English charts only Heather's Coast of Portugal (1800) letters it, across the open water from the Algarve to Cadiz. The gazetteers of 1795–1810 (Brookes, Walker, Cruttwell, the Britannica of 1810) use it for the same bight, but Nelson, the logs and the Naval Chronicle never do (sailors said 'off Cadiz'). Tuckey (1815) says the name was more usually kept for the Bay of Cadiz.
Guadalquivir: the chart letters Guadalquivir, as Cary's Spain (1801) does. The commoner English spelling of 1795–1807 was Guadalquiver: Faden 1807, Heather 1800, Knight c. 1795, Malham and Brookes.

Algeciras: Algeziras on Heather 1800 and Cary 1801 and in the Naval Chronicle of 1805 and Malham. Algesiras is the usual spelling in Nelson's letters of 1805. Algeciras is on Heather's Strait plate after Tofiño (c. 1809) and once in the logs.
Rochefort: Faden 1807, the Naval Chronicle of 1805 and Nicolas's vol. 7 (mostly letters of August–October 1805). Rochfort: Cary 1804, Nicolas's vol. 6 (letters of 1804–05) and Malham.
Cape St Mary: C. St. Mary from Nelson's 'Cape St. Mary' and Faden's 'C. S. Mary'. C. St. Maria on Heather 1800, C. Sta. Maria on Cary 1801.
Cabo da Roca: Rock of Lisbon on Faden 1807, Heather 1800 and Laurie & Whittle 1794 and in Nelson and Malham. C. of Roca on Cary 1801. Cape Roxent in Malham 1795 and Tuckey 1815.
Gulf of Lyons: Cary 1801 and 1804, Nelson, Malham and Brookes. Gulf of Lion is on older charts (La Rochette 1780; Laurie & Whittle 1794).
Douro: Douro on Cary's Portugal (1801) and in Malham and Brookes, for the river at Oporto. Duero on Cary's Europe (1804), the Spanish name of the whole river.
Tangier: Faden 1807, Heather 1800 and c. 1809, Cary 1801, Nelson and Malham. Tangiers on Cary 1804.
Barbadoes: Faden 1807, Cary 1803, Arrowsmith 1803, Nelson and the Naval Chronicle. Barbados on Laurie & Whittle 1794 and once in Malham.
Cape Verde Islands: Arrowsmith 1802. Cape Verd Isles on Faden 1807 and Cary 1805, Cape Verd Islands on Laurie & Whittle 1794; navigation books of 1800–1805 wrote Cape Verd.
Sahara: left unlettered. Period English maps call it Saara or Great Desert (Arrowsmith 1802) or Great Desert of Zaara (Cary 1805); Brookes (1807) writes Zahara.

Forms kept although they look odd today: Bourdeaux (every chart read; Bordeaux only in rare print), Guadaloupe (Faden, Cary 1803, Arrowsmith 1803, Nelson; Guadeloupe on Laurie & Whittle 1794 and in a quarter of the Naval Chronicle's uses), Carthagena (Cary 1804, Nelson, the Naval Chronicle; Cartagena on Faden 1807).
Straits of Gibraltar: 'Straits' on the charts and in naval writing. 'Streights' survived in official documents of 1800–1807 (v-h4), and Faden's 1806 chart title has the singular 'Strait' (h4).

briefRows.brief: Villeneuve breaks out of Toulon on 29 or 30 March 1805 (sources differ)
briefRows.sources: He weighed at about 4 p.m. on 30 March and was a league off Cap Sépet by 7 p.m. (Reille, the Atlas's log and Villeneuve's letter of 9 germinal, in Desbrière 1907, pp. 6–9); Nelson dated it "in the night of Saturday, March 30th". "29 March" is James's one-day slip in converting the Republican date (III 339), copied by Clowes.

briefRows.brief: Collects Spanish ships at Cádiz and crosses to Martinique (beat 2: "gathers Spanish ships at Cádiz")
briefRows.sources: A stop of about six hours on the night of 9–10 April: the French Aigle and six Spanish ships of the line came out, but the Spaniards straggled. Only 14 of the 18 crossed in company; Firme, Terrible and España met Villeneuve at Martinique on 14 May and San Rafael on the 16th (Reille, in Desbrière 1907, pp. 11, 26; Troude III 342; a-h1ac GLYPH-crossing).
briefRows.scene: 14 glyphs on the crossing (4 more apart if stragglers are drawn); 18 at Martinique

briefRows.brief: Villeneuve sails back for Europe around 9 to 11 June
briefRows.sources: He left Martinique on 5 June (James: the 4th), went north past Dominica, Guadeloupe and Antigua, took a convoy off Barbuda on 8 June and turned for Europe on 10 June (Corbett 1910, p. 167; Desbrière 1907, pp. 41–43); his letter is dated at sea on 11 June; James has "the 9th or 10th".
briefRows.scene: Route north through the islands; "10 June" at the turn north of Barbuda

briefRows.brief: Beat 2: "Nelson's route follows, behind"; caption: "Nelson follows him across the Atlantic and back"
briefRows.sources: Homeward the tracks parted. Villeneuve went north of the whole Azores group for Ferrol; Nelson, thinking the allies bound for Cádiz or Toulon, went through the Azores north of São Miguel to Cape St Vincent and Gibraltar (19 July, three days before Finisterre), then north to Ushant (15 August). He never caught up with Villeneuve.
briefRows.scene: Nelson's homeward line runs south of Villeneuve's, to Gibraltar; "and back" holds only loosely

briefRows.brief: Beat 2 caption: "then races back for the Channel"
briefRows.sources: Napoleon's orders of 29 April (brought by the Didon) and Villeneuve's decision of 10 June sent him back to Ferrol first, to gather the ships there before Brest and the Channel (Desbrière 1907, pp. 29, 41–42).
briefRows.scene: The line heads for Ferrol; the caption can keep "for the Channel" as the plan's aim

briefRows.brief: Cape Finisterre, 22 July 1805; beat 3: "Smoke off Cape Finisterre"
briefRows.sources: The fight was 95–130 nm WNW of the cape. Calder's own dispatch puts him at noon at 43°30′ N 11°17′ W (James 43°54′ N 11°38′ W; Desbrière 44°17′ N 11°52′ W at 11.30 a.m.); Corbett's chart (12°20′ W) and the French reckoning (13°53′ W) are too far west (a-h1ac H1-26).
briefRows.scene: Smoke at 43°35′ N 11°40′ W, 113 nm WNW of the cape

briefRows.brief: Villeneuve reaches A Coruña and Ferrol around 1 August
briefRows.sources: He first put into Vigo (anchored at nightfall on 28 July) and left three ships there; he doubled Finisterre on the evening of 1 August and entered the bay on 2 August (Desbrière 1907, p. 86; Corbett 1910, p. 219). The 13 French anchored at A Coruña and the 2 Spaniards went into Ferrol. James and Mahan: 1 August.

briefRows.brief: Instead of heading north for the Channel, he sails south to Cádiz, arriving around 20 August
briefRows.sources: He sailed from Ferrol on 13 August with 29 of the line and stood WNW for two days, turning south only at nightfall on 15 August, about 40 leagues WNW of Finisterre (Reille; Villeneuve wrote 80). He anchored at Cádiz on the evening of 20 August (21 August in the Précis and Escaño's later letter; 17 August in Troude, impossible).

routes.title: Villeneuve, Toulon to Cádiz, 30 March to 9 April 1805 (the leg Stage A draws)
routes.note: Table A of research/scene-02/h1-campaign.md, section 7, as checked in v-h1c.md (H1-35) and ruled in a-h1ac.md (H1-35e). The Atlas's noon latitudes are firm; her longitudes exist only for 1-3 and 10 April, so the other longitudes keep the line in the channels the sources name (est.). Refinements: start in the middle of the Grande Rade (the notes' 43°06'N 5°56'E falls in the inner road on the chart's coast); row 5 lies in the open sea south of the Gulf of Lion and row 6 SE (not SSE) of Barcelona; the Strait at about 11 a.m., not noon; the 4 p.m. point just past Cape Trafalgar, off Conil, at the adjudicated 36°14'N 6°11'W (the task text says 'off Cape Trafalgar rather than off Conil': a-h1ac's final statement puts it just past the cape, off Conil, the same water); an estimated point in the offing keeps the line about 3 nm off Cádiz's rocky west shore; the anchoring in open water about 3.2 nm west of Las Puercas and 2.5 nm west of the Los Cochinos buoy, outside the entrance shoals (Corbett: outside the bay), not in the outer-bay berth of August-October. Dropped as adding nothing to the shape: the notes' estimated points east of Cabo de la Nao, off Garrucha and south of Málaga (the line keeps at least 3.5 nm off those coasts without them). Checked against Natural Earth 10m: the drawn curve keeps 2.2 nm or more from every cape (Cap Cépet 2.2, the coast east of Cartagena 2.5, Punta Cires about 2.5, Tarifa 4.1, Cape Trafalgar 4.9, Europa Point 6.4, Cape Spartel 10, Las Puercas 3.2, Cádiz west shore 2.8); only the leg out of Toulon road runs within 1 nm of the shore, as any exit from the road must.

routes.title: Villeneuve, return to Europe, Cape Finisterre and Vigo, 10 June to 28 July 1805
routes.note: Table D: Corbett's chart after Desbrière (±0.3°) with the Sally's noon position (British DR). Daily marks stop on 24 June; the line then runs straight to Corvo (2 July, Reille). Left out: the Curieux's 19 June position (the British report's 33°12'N 58°W lies two days ahead of the chart's marks; the chart's circle 30°13'N 58°06'W is on the line), James's 30 June point NE of Corvo (it would double back before Reille's 2 July sighting), the doubtful noon of 23 July (journal 43°41'N, 12°48' from Paris) and the 40 leagues WSW of Finisterre of the 27 July letter (a hairpin). The Z of 9-20 July is real, not reckoning noise: a NE gale on the 9th, the nearest approach west of Oporto on the 12th, then four days driven back west (Corbett 1910, p. 195); drop 12 and 16 July for a plain line. The action point is a-h1ac's smoke position. The entry to Vigo is by the south mouth of the ría (est.; the Cíes are not in Natural Earth); inside the ría the line runs 1-2 nm from the shore. Open-sea segments 2 nm or more from land (Corvo 13 nm, Cape Finisterre 38 nm).

routes.note: Table F, corrected by a-h1b.md (Palmas 26-30 March, Pula 31 March-3 April, off Palermo 9-10 April not Ustica on the 7th, Lagos 9-11 May, the bear-away point SE of the cape). The line starts at Pula: the Palmas-Pula-Toro moves would double back along Sardinia's south coast. It loops to Palermo and back (two control points north of Capo San Vito keep the curve 8 nm or more off the cape; without them it crossed the cape). No positions were recorded on the beat west of 19-30 April (est.). Tetuan is entered and left as anchorages are; at Gibraltar the line touches the mouth of the bay (Nelson anchored there from 2 to 6 p.m. on 6 May), about 2 nm from Europa Point and Punta Carnero. Open-sea segments 2 nm or more from land.

North of the Azores the 8 July log fix (São Miguel ESE by compass, 17½ leagues, computed with 21.1° W) replaces the chart's mark, and a-h1b's control point at 37°58'N 26°05'W keeps the line 3.3 nm off São Miguel's north coast (the route went through the islands, north of São Miguel). Dropped as zigzags: 24 June (31°43'N 52°56'W, a doubling back 70 nm west of the line) and 4 and 6 July (wobbles of 14-28 nm in the calms). The 13 July signal-log bearing does not fit and is not used. The last points take the line through the Strait, south of Punta Carnero, into Gibraltar Bay.

routes.title: Nelson, Gibraltar to Ushant and Spithead, 22 July to 18 August 1805
routes.note: Table J: estimates to Cape St Vincent, then Faden's marks as Corbett redrew them, with the diary's positions of 3 and 7 August (Desbrière 1907, pp. 74-75, read on the page images). Dropped as zigzags: 2, 4, 5 and 6 August (tacks against the northerlies, up to 30 nm either side of the line between the two diary positions). Left out: the Tetuan call of 22-25 July (a 25-nm spur). The Channel legs are estimates round St Catherine's Point and the east end of the Isle of Wight to Spithead. Open-sea segments 2 nm or more from land.

openDoubts: Dating of the crossing: Desbrière's second Atlas table may carry printed dates or the noon of the day after (a-h1ac H1-07, genuinely disputed), so the crossing has no day marks.

The Curieux's sighting on 19 June: 33°12′ N 58° W by Bettesworth's report (Corbett 1910, p. 181; James III 354) or about 30°13′ N 58°06′ W on Corbett's chart after Desbrière's; the report puts the fleet two days ahead of the chart's daily marks.
Where Villeneuve's five frigates rejoined: about 20 leagues NE of Corvo on 30 June (James) against Corvo first sighted on 2 July (Reille).
The turn for Europe: 10 June (Corbett; Desbrière's 'dès le 10 juin') or 11 June (Villeneuve's letter dated at sea; Desbrière's 'mettait à la voile le 11 juin'); James has 'the 9th or 10th'.
The Didon's arrival at Martinique: 29 May (Mahan), 30 May (Reille), 31 May (Corbett) or 1 June (James).
Nelson off Palermo turned west on 9 April (his letter of 18 April) or 10 April (his letter dated off Palermo that day).
Where Donald Campbell gave Nelson his intelligence: as Nelson passed the Strait on 6 May (Campbell's own complaint, Nicolas VI 431 n.; Corbett, James, Clowes) or at Lagos (Mahan, Desbrière).
How many of Cochrane's ships Dacres kept at Jamaica: four (James, Clowes) or five of six (Corbett); Nelson's 12 at Barbados is not affected. Amphion's parting on the way home is not recorded.
Nelson's 13 July signal-log bearing (Cape St Vincent S 89° E, 183 leagues) does not fit Faden's track for that day; unresolved.

Finisterre: the British noon position (Calder 43°30′ N 11°17′ W; James 43°54′ N 11°38′ W; Desbrière 44°17′ N 11°52′ W at 11.30 a.m.); when the firing stopped (about 7.30, Desbrière; nine, Calder at his trial; 9.30, James); when the prizes struck (soon after 8 p.m., British; daybreak on the 23rd, French); allied losses (476 James, 496 Corbett, about 580 Desbrière's footnote).
Vigo: the Cíes sighted at 6 p.m. on 27 or 28 July (Desbrière's sentence is ambiguous); the 27 July letter's 40 leagues WSW of Finisterre fits neither well.
A Coruña: 2 August (Desbrière, from the French records; Corbett for the junction) or 1 August (James, Mahan, Corbett's narrative).

Where Villeneuve turned south on 15 August: 40 leagues WNW of Finisterre at noon (Reille), 80 leagues (Villeneuve; impossible, says Corbett), near 44°40′ N 12°25′ W (Desbrière's staff map, rejected by Corbett); James implies the evening of the 14th. The turning point drawn is an estimate.

20 August: off Cape St Vincent on the 17th (Desbrière's text) or 18th (James; Desbrière's map); who led the chase of Collingwood (Magon, Desbrière; Gravina, Corbett); Collingwood back off Cádiz that evening with four (Desbrière) or before daylight on the 21st (James); the 10 a.m. position 36°13′ N 6°42′ W if 'Cádiz NE nine leagues' is true, about 36°07′ N 6°32′ W if by compass.
Strength at Cádiz: British about 26 from 30 August (James III 379) or 32 (Desbrière, who counts some ships twice); allied 35 in port (James) against Collingwood's 36 'men-of-war' (all classes).
The Toulon berth, the 9 April anchorage outside Cádiz bay and the 4 p.m. point off Conil are estimates: no source gives them.

ownerQuestions: Villeneuve's homeward line: keep the real Z of 9–20 July west of Portugal (a north-east gale, the nearest approach west of Oporto, then four days driven back west), or draw a plain line by dropping the 12 and 16 July points?

Nelson's line after the West Indies: end it at Gibraltar (19 July), or carry it on north to Ushant and Spithead (15–18 August) as the sources have it? And should the beat 2 caption keep 'races back for the Channel' and 'across the Atlantic and back', which describe the plan's aim and only loosely Nelson's track (Villeneuve made for Ferrol; Nelson went home by Gibraltar)?

On the crossing, show 14 glyphs (the body that crossed together) or 18 (all that reached Martinique), and should the minor moments the research supports be drawn at all: Orde's six drawing off from Cádiz on 9 April, the four Spanish stragglers, and the Curieux's sighting of 19 June?
